name: Apple cider vinegar for odour
lead: Applying apple cider vinegar to the skin, typically the underarms, is a folk remedy people use to keep body odour down so they smell fresher and cleaner. It is a low-cost, kitchen-cupboard alternative to commercial deodorant and appears in natural-grooming routines. Apple cider vinegar is about 5% acetic acid in water, made by fermenting apple cider.[1]

Underarm odour arises mainly when skin bacteria break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands, rather than from sweat itself.[2] Corynebacterium species make lipases that break sweat lipids into odorous molecules such as butyric acid, and Staphylococcus species produce other odour compounds.[2] Believers say vinegar's acidity makes skin less hospitable to these bacteria; no published trials were found testing apple cider vinegar for this purpose.[1][3]
Wikipedia reports that evidence for apple cider vinegar's health claims in general is poor and that applying it to skin may cause burns.[1]

chain: Acidic vinegar wiped on the underarm skin
Skin becomes less hospitable to odour-causing bacteria (as proponents say)
Less underarm odour and a fresher scent
angle.text: People wipe diluted vinegar on the underarms as a home deodorant, saying its acidity discourages the bacteria that create odour. The payoff they seek is smelling clean without commercial products.

paras: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice to alcohol and then converting it to acetic acid; unfiltered versions can retain a bacterial biofilm called the mother.[1] The practice of wiping it on skin to deodorise is shared as a home remedy and is part of broader natural-deodorant culture.

Skin bacteria rather than sweat itself cause most underarm odour.[2] Apocrine glands, concentrated in the armpits and active from puberty, secrete the compounds that skin flora metabolise into smelly substances.[2] Corynebacterium jeikeium is described as more common in men's armpits and linked to a rancid, cheese-like smell, while Staphylococcus haemolyticus is more common in women and linked to a fruitier, onion-like odour.[2]

Standard measures described include bathing with antibacterial soap, deodorants that reduce odour without reducing sweating, and antiperspirants with aluminium salts that block sweat pores; surgery is reserved for severe cases.[2]

Proponents hold that vinegar's acidity lowers skin pH and makes it less hospitable to odour-causing bacteria. Wikipedia's deodorant article describes acid-based products as aiming to preserve the skin's acid mantle, which limits bacterial growth.[3]

Wikipedia reports no high-quality clinical evidence for apple cider vinegar's claimed benefits, and says major health organisations do not recommend it for therapeutic use.[1] No studies of its effect on body odour were found.
Applying it to skin to treat skin conditions may cause burns, and using vinegar as a topical medication is described as hazardous.[1] Commercial brands vary in acid content.[1]

timeline.event: A cookbook includes recipes for apple cider vinegar, reflecting its early-1800s popularity.[1]

lore.intro: Apple cider vinegar is discussed in natural-grooming communities as a cheap, home remedy for odour.

claims.claim: Wiping vinegar on the underarms removes or prevents body odour
claims.believers: Proponents say its acidity discourages the bacteria that create odour and that it is a low-cost alternative to commercial deodorant.
claims.experts: No published studies have tested apple cider vinegar for odour; reference sources report poor evidence for its health claims and note it can burn skin when applied.[1]

card.summary: A home remedy of wiping vinegar on skin to curb odour; untested for this use, with burn warnings.

quick.overview:
Some people wipe apple cider vinegar on the underarms or body to reduce odour. It is a folk remedy tied to natural-grooming culture.

No published study has tested it for odour, and reference sources report poor evidence for its health claims generally.
quick.mechanism: People say the acetic acid lowers skin pH and makes the skin less hospitable to odour-causing bacteria, which break down apocrine sweat.
quick.risks: Reference sources say applying it to skin may cause burns. Acid content varies between commercial brands.
